title: The Head of Department Manifesto
author: Dominic Salles
summary: In the introductory chapter of a serialized book he is writing in public, veteran head of department and school improvement consultant Dominic Salles argues that roughly 70% of secondary schools remain stubbornly average not because of laziness but because leaders conflate 'teaching' and 'learning,' pouring energy into consistency-producing rituals (entry routines, uniform checks, green pens) that are easy to observe but weakly connected to actual student progress. His central claim, delivered as a three-part mission statement -- build a team that helps students master your subject so they make great progress -- is meant to function as a checklist any leadership decision can be run against, deliberately modeled on Atul Gawande's The Checklist Manifesto, which argues that in complex environments a simple checklist outperforms even expert judgment. Salles's most provocative move is arguing that 'great teaching' itself is largely a myth as an explanatory variable: since genuinely excellent teachers use wildly different personal styles and techniques (he cites Doug Lemov's own Teach Like a Champion expanding from 49 to 62 techniques, none of which any single teacher masters), the real driver of student progress is not what a teacher does but what a curriculum requires students to do, making curriculum design, not teaching-technique observation, the higher-leverage lever for a department leader to pull. He backs the broader critique of school-leadership advice with Robert Coe's finding that much cited leadership research contains serious methodological flaws, positioning his own three-pillar framework (team, curriculum, impact) as a corrective built from outside-education sources (Gawande, and Steven Bartlett's The Diary of a CEO) rather than from the education-leadership literature he considers largely unverified.
points: The essay's sharpest diagnostic move is naming the substitution leaders routinely make -- 'what we can make consistent' in place of 'what actually impacts learning' -- to explain why so much visible leadership effort (uniform checks, entry routines, green pens) coexists with persistently average outcomes.

Its most provocative claim is that 'great teaching' is the wrong unit of analysis entirely: since genuinely excellent teachers use radically different personal styles (even Doug Lemov's own technique list has grown from 49 to 62, none fully mastered by any one teacher), the actual driver of student mastery is what the curriculum requires students to do, not what the teacher does.

Robert Coe's finding that a significant part of the school-leadership research literature 'contains methodological flaws that make its claims untrustworthy' is used to justify deliberately building the framework from outside-education sources (Gawande's checklist theory, Bartlett's business podcast) rather than the leadership literature Salles considers unreliable.

The three-part mission statement functions as an explicit decision-filter, not a slogan: every leadership choice is meant to be run against whether it improves the team, improves subject mastery, or improves student progress, giving middle leaders a falsifiable test rather than a vague aspiration.
quotes: Roughly 70% of secondary schools sit comfortably in the middle, generating entirely average Progress 8 scores year after year. This is not because teachers are lazy or because school leaders lack ambition.
In the day-to-day cyclone of middle leadership, we routinely substitute "what we can make consistent" for "what actually impacts learning".
To build a team that helps your students master your subject so that they can make great progress.
If teaching is the main thing causing students to learn more, then great teachers would use the same techniques -- but they don't.

A significant part of the school leadership literature, including some of the most cited and influential studies, contains methodological flaws that make its claims untrustworthy... Much of the plentiful and eagerly attended advice that is given is not clear, actionable or scientifically verified.
So, focus on the 'stuff' of learning -- the curriculum -- and you will lead a fantastic team. Focus on their teaching and things might improve, but it will be painfully slow.
